construction.overview: Typical construction for this class of table fan combines a weighted cast pedestal, an enclosed motor housing, a riveted blade hub, and a wire guard. Visible in this frontal view are the wire guard cage (part-1), four pitched blades and hub (part-2), central medallion (part-3), flared pedestal base and mount (part-4), and the cylindrical motor housing behind the blades (part-5). The internal motor and wiring (part-6) are not visible and are inferred only from typology; no dimensions, materials, wiring or internal geometry can be verified from the image alone.

stages.title: Pedestal Base Formation and Mounting
stages.description: Typical practice forms the flared base (part-4) from cast metal for mass and rigidity, then machines the foot flat for stability and drills mounting points for the pedestal neck. Visible flanged foot and side fasteners suggest a bolted joint to the museum plinth, with alignment of the vertical neck critical to keep the fan head upright; heavy base material lowers center of gravity to resist tipping.

stages.title: Motor Housing Integration (Inferred Internals)
stages.description: The cylindrical housing (part-5) typically encloses the electric drive (part-6) and provides a rigid bearing support aligned to the pedestal neck. Conceptually the housing is joined to the pedestal via a clamped or threaded neck, with the motor shaft axis centered to the housing bore. Material stiffness matters for vibration control. Internal motor type, windings and wiring are not visible and are not specified here - only that the housing would functionally contain and locate the drive without detailing electrical connections.

stages.title: Blade Hub and Pitch Assembly
stages.description: Four blades (part-2) are typically stamped from sheet metal, given a consistent pitch twist, and riveted to a central hub. Visible rivets and notched blade tips suggest factory balancing and attachment. The red medallion (part-3) covers the hub fastener. Pitch angle and uniform radial alignment are critical for axial airflow and to avoid wobble; painted steel or aluminum alloy is typical for light weight and corrosion resistance, but exact material is not verified.

stages.title: Wire Guard Cage Assembly and Final Alignment
stages.description: The spherical guard (part-1) is typically made by bending and spot-welding concentric wire rings to radial wire supports, then finishing with paint. It is conceptually attached to the motor housing rim with screws or clips, surrounding the blades with clearance to prevent contact while allowing through-flow. Visible concentric rings and bent supports indicate this construction, with even spacing and secure fixing essential for guard rigidity and blade clearance.

checks: Check actual footprint diameter and mass of base needed for tipping resistance - not measurable from photo
Check blade pitch angle, blade mass and balance, and hub concentricity
Check guard wire spacing, weld integrity and attachment method to housing
Check motor condition, insulation integrity and whether unit is operational - requires professional inspection, do not energize
Check for missing fasteners, surface finish condition, restoration or modifications

Verified material specifications and finish thickness for all metal parts

learning.title: Paper Pitch and Flared Pedestal Model of the Vintage GE Table Fan
learning.answer: This tabletop project demonstrates two principles visible in the vintage GE fan: how a flared pedestal base provides tipping resistance, and how angled blades create axial-flow direction. A folded paper vane shows pitch concept and a cardboard base shows stability, relating to part-2, part-4 and part-5. The model is static and hand-moved, does not generate or measure real airflow, and is a conceptual illustration only, not a functional fan. This proposal has not been physically tested; the observation can fail without danger if folds are imprecise.

materials.purpose: Forms flared pedestal base demonstrator for stability test
Forms folded pitched vanes to illustrate blade angle and axial direction concept
Forms short vertical neck to show alignment between base and fan head
Secures folds and joins for base and vane without cutting tools
Acts as hand-held handle to move paper vane and observe orientation

steps.title: Form the flared base
steps.instruction: Take a pre-sized square of cardboard about hand-size, fold edges under slightly to create a flat stable foot, then tape a small folded cardboard ring on top to mark the pedestal center. No cutting needed; fold or tear to shape.
steps.observe: Base sits flat on table and does not rock when tapped lightly.

steps.title: Add the upright support
steps.instruction: Stand a short paper straw vertically on the cardboard base center and secure with adhesive tape around its lower end to represent the pedestal neck and motor housing alignment.
steps.observe: Straw stays upright and centered; tape holds it without obstructing the base edge.

steps.title: Fold a pitch-angle vane
steps.instruction: Take a small rectangle of paper, fold a gentle diagonal crease across its width to create two angled facets like pitched blades, then tape the paper to the side of the pencil near the end as a hand-held demonstrator. Keep it static, not spinning.
steps.observe: Paper shows an obvious angled surface relative to the pencil axis, visible from front and side.

steps.title: Test pedestal stability
steps.instruction: Place the straw-on-base assembly on table and gently nudge its top sideways and from different directions, comparing to nudging a single pencil standing alone.
steps.observe: Wider cardboard base resists tipping more than the narrow pencil alone; it returns to flat or slides rather than immediately toppling.

steps.title: Demonstrate axial direction concept by hand motion
steps.instruction: Hold the pencil with paper vane and slowly push it straight forward through air while watching the angled facets; then pull it backward.
steps.observe: Angled facets face forward on push and backward on pull, illustrating conceptually how pitch determines intended airflow direction along the axis. No measurable wind is expected from this small hand movement; if fold is flat, no direction is visible and the demonstration simply shows need for pitch.

safety_notes: Do not attempt to power, disassemble or modify the real antique fan; degraded insulation can be hazardous
Keep small paper and tape pieces away from young children
If using binder clips as alternative, keep clips away from skin and eyes
Use only folding and tearing by hand; no blades, heat or tools needed
limitations: Does not reproduce electrical drive, rotation, airflow, noise or weight of the real metal fan
Paper folds only suggest pitch concept; they do not prove aerodynamic performance and resemblance is not proof of function
Cardboard base shows stability principle at tabletop scale only, not the actual cast-metal mass or tipping forces
Model has no functional guard; paper guard would not provide protection as the real wire cage (part-1) is intended to
Proposed model has not been physically tested; observation may fail if folds are inaccurate but can be retried safely without modification to the original object
